beats.narration_text: Vanakkam. This is Liam, in for Bear, with chapter one of INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about one test for any claim about a model: what result would make it false? A claim counts only if it names that result. You'll see each claim drawn as the outcomes it forbids. The trap: a claim nothing could refute looks, on a dashboard, just like one that passed.

show.event: 'TL;DR.' wordmark; 'Vanakkam, Liam'; the course line; heading
line 1 lands on 'a claim counts only'
line 2 lands on 'drawn as the outcomes it forbids'

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: The dashboard says the system is robust. What would it look like if it weren't?
lines: A claim counts only if it names the result that would make it false.
You'll see each claim drawn as the region of outcomes it forbids.
The trap: a claim nothing could refute looks just like one that passed.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Every model you ship or buy arrives with claims like robust, performs well, a success. If a claim forbids nothing, no test can ever catch the model failing. A sepsis model passed every check its builders chose, and still missed roughly two in three septic patients. Write the forbidden result first, and a test can finally say no.

“The system is robust.”
What result would

beats.narration_text: Four terms you'll hear. A held-out test set: data kept aside during training, used only to test the model. Recall: of the real cases, the share the model catches. Precision: of the cases the model flags, the share that are real. And out-of-distribution: inputs unlike the data the model learned from.

learn.question: The dashboard says robust. What would it look like if it weren't?
learn.action: Drop three very different results onto the outcome axis under the claim.
learn.observation: The claim survives all three, including the terrible one.
learn.inference: A claim that survives everything has not been tested by anything.
learn.next_question: What would the same claim look like if it could fail?

beats.narration_text: A dashboard tile says: the system is robust. Under it, an axis: the error rate on unfamiliar inputs, from none on the left to a lot on the right. Now let results come in. A low error rate. Robust. A middling one. Still robust. A terrible one. Nobody wrote down what would count against it, so — still robust. So what would non-robust look like?

shot.visual_intent: The claim tile 'The system is robust.' lands at top; the outcome axis draws below (error rate on unfamiliar inputs, none → a lot, no numbers); three constructed observation dots drop onto the axis — left, middle, far right — and after each a tally 'compatible: n of n' updates; a small dim caption 'constructed observations'; the question lands.

show.event: question: what would non-robust look like?

shot.motion_claim: The key case, unsolved: every result fits a claim that forbids nothing.

learn.question: What does 'robust' look like when it could fail?
learn.action: Rewrite the claim with a metric, threshold and window; shade what it forbids; replay the results.
learn.observation: Two of the three results land in the forbidden region.
learn.inference: Only a claim that forbids something can be refuted — or survive a real test.
learn.next_question: Is that a trick of this one claim, or does it work on another?

beats.narration_text: Rewrite it the way the chapter's table does: error rate on out-of-distribution inputs stays below two percent, across a thirty-day rolling window. Put a mark at two percent. Everything past it is now forbidden — shade it. Replay the same three results. The first fits. The second lands in the shaded part. So does the third. Either one refutes it. The claim can now be wrong, which means it finally says something.

shot.visual_intent: The tile morphs from 'The system is robust.' into the two-line Popperian form; a tick at 0% and 2% appear on the SAME axis; the region right of 2% shades (dim fill, 'forbidden' label inside); the three dots replay — dot 1 stays left of the mark, dots 2 and 3 land inside the region; a terracotta dot marks 'refuted' beside the tally.

show.event: tile morphs to the table's correction
the three dots replay; two land inside

shot.motion_claim: Instance one, moving: the same axis and the same results, one change — the claim now forbids a region.

learn.question: Does the move work on a different claim?
learn.action: Rewrite 'performs well' with the table's precision and recall floors; redraw on a recall axis.
learn.observation: The forbidden region moves to the left — below 0.88.
learn.inference: Where the region sits depends on the claim; that it exists is the whole point.
learn.next_question: So how do people usually check a claim like 'performs well'?

beats.narration_text: Second row. The model performs well. The table's rewrite: precision at least point nine one, and recall at least point eight eight, on the held-out test set, evaluated monthly. Swap the axis to recall — the share of real cases caught. Watch the forbidden region move: now it is everything below point eight eight, on the left. Different claim, different side. Same move: the claim is the region it rules out.

shot.visual_intent: The dots clear; the tile morphs to 'The model performs well.' then to its correction (precision ≥ 0.91 · recall ≥ 0.88 · monthly); the axis label morphs to 'recall', ticks 0 · 0.88 · 1; the shaded region slides and re-sizes from the right side to [0, 0.88) on the left.

show.event: the region slides to the left side

shot.motion_claim: Instance two, moving: vary one thing (the claim); the forbidden region morphs to the other side.

learn.question: How do people usually decide a model works?
learn.action: Stack the favorable checks the chapter lists and let each raise a confidence bar.
learn.observation: The bar climbs with every check and never reaches the top.
learn.inference: Confirming instances pile up without providing certainty.
learn.next_question: Then what kind of evidence could actually settle it?

beats.narration_text: Now the usual way to check a model. Take the sepsis early-warning model the chapter opens with, and count the evidence that it works. Strong internal validation. A respectable reported A U C. A risk number on every patient. Published. Cleared through procurement. Each one pushes confidence up. But look at the top of the bar: however many you stack, it never reaches certain. Five white swans do not prove that every swan is white.

shot.visual_intent: The region fades (the axis stays, ghosted); the tile reads 'The sepsis model performs well.'; five checks write on at left one per spoken item, each with an ink dot; beside them a confidence bar grows a step per check toward a dashed 'certain' line at the top and never reaches it; dim caption 'confidence: schematic, not measured'.

show.event: tile: the sepsis model performs well
five checks land, one per spoken item
the bar steps up with each
the bar stops short of the dashed top

shot.motion_claim: The natural approach walked to its limit: confirmations stack without ever reaching certainty.

learn.question: What kind of evidence could settle 'performs well'?
learn.action: Ask what the claim forbids; draw it as a region on the recall axis.
learn.observation: As written it forbids nothing; with a recall floor it forbids everything below 0.88.
learn.inference: Only a result inside the forbidden region can test the claim.
learn.next_question: What happens when a real result arrives?

beats.narration_text: So stop asking how much evidence the claim has. Ask what it forbids. The model performs well — what recall would count against it? Nothing was written down, so the whole axis is allowed, and every check can only confirm. Now borrow the table's row: recall at least point eight eight. Everything below it goes dark. That is the claim, drawn: the outcomes it rules out.

shot.visual_intent: The five check labels fade and their dots slide into a compact column beside the bar; the recall axis returns to ink with the whole axis marked 'allowed' (no region); then the 0.88 tick and the forbidden region [0, 0.88) grow in from the axis; dim caption 'threshold: the table's row, applied'.

show.event: labels fade; the five dots slide beside the bar
0.88 tick; the region below it grows

shot.motion_claim: The representation: a claim is the region of outcomes it forbids — now on the sepsis case.

learn.question: Where will the external result land, and what will it do to the bar?
learn.action: Hold the hovering result above the axis and ask the viewer to commit.
learn.observation: The viewer commits a position and a bar height.
learn.inference: A prediction turns the drop into evidence.

beats.narration_text: Then a team at the University of Michigan checked the model against what actually happened to twenty-seven thousand, six hundred ninety-seven hospitalized patients, at a health system that had not built it. Before the result lands — commit. Where on this axis does it fall? And what happens to the confidence bar?

shot.visual_intent: A terracotta dot appears above the axis, hovering, with the label 'Michigan: 27,697 patients'; a dashed guide drops from it toward the axis; everything else holds still; caption 'commit before it lands'.

show.event: the external result hovers above the axis

learn.question: What does one result inside the forbidden region do?
learn.action: Drop the Michigan result onto the axis.
learn.observation: It lands at about one third, inside the region; the stacked confidence goes to zero.
learn.inference: One falsifying instance settles what no number of confirmations could.
learn.next_question: Does this work on every claim in the table?

beats.narration_text: It caught roughly one in three. Deep inside the shaded region. And the bar — five confirmations — falls to nothing. Five white swans. One black one. Settled.

shot.visual_intent: The terracotta dot drops onto the axis at recall ≈ 1/3, deep in the forbidden region; label 'caught ≈ 1 in 3'; the confidence bar's fill shrinks to zero; the five confirmation dots dim to ghost; 'refuted' lands beside the tile.
shot.motion_claim: The aha: the two threads collide — the forbidden region and the swan count — in one continuous drop; narration short.

learn.question: Does the move work on every claim in the table?
learn.action: Rewrite each of the four rhetorical claims with its metric, threshold and window.
learn.observation: Every left cell forbids nothing; every right cell carves a region.
learn.inference: The move is general: name the result that would make it false.
learn.next_question: What do we call a claim in the right-hand form?

beats.narration_text: Now the move is quick. Line up the chapter's four claims. Robust becomes: error below two percent over thirty days. Performs well becomes: precision and recall floors. The migration was a success becomes: zero data-loss events, and ninety-fifth percentile latency at most a hundred and twenty milliseconds, forty-eight hours after cutover. We have mitigated drift becomes: P S I on the three highest-weight features below point one zero, week over week. Left column: nothing forbidden. Right column: every cell carves a region.

shot.visual_intent: A two-column table builds row by row: left 'forbids nothing' (the four rhetorical claims), right 'forbids a region' (the four corrections); a column rule draws; beside each right cell a small dim shaded block grows — the carved region — while the left cells get none; dim caption 'PSI is named here, not taught'.
shot.motion_claim: Developing the insight: the same move on four claims; what varies is the region, what stays is that it exists.

learn.question: What do we call a claim that names what would make it false?
learn.action: Name it and set the two evidence columns side by side.
learn.observation: Confirmations never reach certainty; one refutation does.
learn.inference: Falsifiable claims are the only ones a test can speak to.
learn.next_question: So what was wrong with the dashboard tile we started with?

beats.narration_text: This deserves its name. A claim is falsifiable when it names the observation that would make it false. And notice the asymmetry you just watched. Confirming results pile up without ever reaching certainty. One falsifying result settles it. You can't prove a model works in all cases. You can prove it fails in this one.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the five ink dots in a column with an upward arrow that stops short of a dashed 'certain' line — 'confirmations pile up'; right: the one terracotta dot — 'one refutation settles it'; a divider draws between; then 'falsifiable' lands bold with its one-line definition beneath.

show.event: left: dots + arrow short of certain
right: the one dot settles it

shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives last, as the name for what was watched; no equation, so no tangent.

learn.question: What was wrong with 'the system is robust'?
learn.action: Return to the first tile and draw the line it never had.
learn.observation: Without the line every result fits; with it, results can refute.
learn.inference: 'Unrefuted' and 'validated' look identical until the claim forbids something.

beats.narration_text: Back to the dashboard. The system is robust. It survived every result because it forbade none. On a dashboard, a claim that survived a real test and a claim that was never at risk look identical. Draw the two-percent line, and the same results can finally say no. Not taught here: writing that line before you read the output. That part is yours.

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK state returns — tile 'The system is robust.', the error-rate axis, the three constructed dots, 'compatible: 3 of 3'; a twin tile 'validated' appears beside it, identical in form — 'look identical'; then the 2% mark and the forbidden region grow on the same axis and the far dots land inside it; dim caption 'not taught here: the line first'.

show.event: twin tiles: survived a test vs never at risk
the 2% region grows; two dots now inside

shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's objects resolve; the boundary names the transfer exercise.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A claim counts only in the form that names the result that would make it false. Draw it as the outcomes it forbids: robust forbids nothing; error below two percent over thirty days carves a region. Confirmations pile up without certainty; one refutation settles it. The sepsis model's checks were white swans; one external test on twenty-seven thousand patients was the black one. And on a dashboard, unrefuted and validated look the same.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: A team reports: Our model achieves 94% accuracy on the held-out test set. Before anything else, predict: what result would make this claim false, as written? Then rewrite it the Popperian way, naming a metric, a threshold and a measurement window, and draw what it forbids as a shaded region on a number line. Finally, describe one way the model could perform badly that the original sentence would never catch. Two things to look for. Did it write a threshold and a window, not just 'accuracy should be high'? And did it say what the claim forbids before it said anything about whether the claim is true?
